name: Shoulder pendulum
why: Moves the shoulder joint gently while the muscles stay relaxed, because gravity and your body's sway do the work. It eases pain and keeps the joint moving when lifting the arm hurts, as in the painful early stage of frozen shoulder.
setup: Stand next to a table, desk or chair back and lean forward, supporting yourself with your good hand.
Let the sore arm hang straight down, completely relaxed.
cues: Sway your body to swing the arm
Small circles, then a little bigger
mistakes: Using the shoulder muscles to swing the arm
Swinging so big that it hurts
Rounding the back instead of hinging at the hips
feel: A loose, gentle swinging in the shoulder. A mild stretch is fine.
stopIf: Pain is sharp or keeps building while you do it.
cautions: After shoulder surgery, follow your surgeon's or physio's instructions on when to start.

name: Table slide (shoulder flexion)
why: Takes the shoulder forward and up while the table carries the arm's weight, so you can work on range without straining the muscles. A good next step after pendulums when the shoulder is stiff.
setup: Sit facing a table with your sore-side hand resting on a small towel on the table.
Sit tall, feet flat on the floor.
cues: Lean your body forward to help
mistakes: Hitching the shoulder up towards the ear
feel: A gentle stretch under the arm or around the shoulder at the end of the slide.
stopIf: Pain is sharp, or aching lasts more than about an hour afterwards.

name: Assisted arm raise with stick
why: Your good arm lifts the sore arm overhead using a stick, so the shoulder moves through its range without its own muscles fighting the stiffness.
setup: Lie on your back with knees bent.
Hold a stick or broom handle in both hands, hands shoulder-width apart, resting on your thighs.
mistakes: Arching the back to get further
feel: A stretch in the shoulder and under the arm at the top of the movement.
stopIf: Sharp pain, or aching that lasts more than about an hour afterwards.

name: Assisted outward rotation with stick
why: Turning the arm outwards is usually the most restricted movement in frozen shoulder. The stick lets your good arm gently push the sore arm into rotation.
setup: Lie on your back with the sore elbow bent to 90 degrees and tucked against your side, a small folded towel under the elbow.
Hold a stick in both hands, the sore hand gripping one end.
cues: Good arm pushes the hand outwards
mistakes: Letting the elbow drift away from your side
Lifting the shoulder off the floor
feel: A stretch at the front of the shoulder.
stopIf: Sharp pain, or aching that lasts more than about an hour afterwards.

name: Towel stretch behind the back
why: Helps you reach behind your back again (tucking in a shirt, fastening a bra), one of the last movements to come back after a stiff shoulder.
setup: Hold a towel over your good shoulder with the good hand.
Reach the sore hand behind your back and hold the bottom of the towel.
cues: Good hand pulls the towel up
Let the sore hand slide up your back
feel: A stretch at the front and top of the sore shoulder.
stopIf: Sharp pain, or aching that lasts more than about an hour afterwards.

name: Cross-body shoulder stretch
why: Stretches the back of the shoulder, which tightens in frozen shoulder and with lots of sitting, and can pinch the front of the shoulder when you lift your arm.
setup: Stand or sit tall.
Bring one arm across your chest at shoulder height and hold it above the elbow with the other hand.
cues: Ease the arm across your chest
mistakes: Pulling on the elbow joint itself
feel: A stretch at the back of the shoulder.
stopIf: Pinching pain at the front or top of the shoulder.

name: Wall finger walk
why: Lets you gain range a little at a time and see it. Mark your highest point: watching it climb week by week is a great motivator.
setup: Stand facing a wall, about an arm's length away.
Place the fingertips of the sore arm on the wall at waist height.
cues: Walk your fingers up the wall
feel: A stretch in the shoulder and under the arm at the top.

name: Outward rotation hold (isometric)
why: Works the rotator cuff muscles that turn the arm outwards without moving the joint: a gentle, pain-friendly way to start strengthening.
setup: Stand side-on to a wall or door frame, working side nearest, elbow bent to 90 degrees and tucked against your side.
Place the back of the wrist against the wall.
cues: Press the back of your hand into the wall
mistakes: Letting the elbow leave your side
feel: Effort at the back of the shoulder.

name: Band outward rotation
why: Strengthens the rotator cuff muscles that keep the ball of the shoulder centred in its socket when you lift and reach.
setup: Anchor a band at elbow height and stand side-on, working arm away from the anchor.
Elbow bent to 90 degrees and tucked against a small folded towel at your side, holding the band.
mistakes: Elbow drifting away from the body
Using a band that's too strong
feel: Effort at the back of the shoulder.
stopIf: Sharp pain, or pain that's worse the next day.

name: Band row
why: Strengthens the upper back and the muscles that hold your shoulder blades, supporting both the neck and the shoulders.
setup: Anchor a band at chest height (shut in a door or round a post).
Hold an end in each hand, arms straight in front, and step back until the band is tight.
feel: Work between your shoulder blades and at the back of the shoulders.
stopIf: Pain spreads into your arm, or neck pain increases.

name: Doorway chest stretch
why: Opens up the chest muscles that tighten when you sit rounded forward, making it easier to sit and stand tall without straining the neck.
setup: Stand in a doorway with your forearms on the door frame, elbows at about shoulder height.
Step one foot forward.
mistakes: Elbows too high if it pinches
feel: A stretch across the front of the chest and shoulders.
stopIf: Pinching at the front of the shoulder, or tingling in the arms or hands.

name: Forearm wall slide
why: Raises the arms overhead with the wall's support while training the shoulder blades to move well: a bridge between stretching and strengthening.
setup: Stand facing a wall with your forearms on it, elbows at shoulder height, little fingers touching the wall.
cues: Slide your forearms up the wall
Let the shoulder blades rotate up
mistakes: Forcing the top of the range
feel: Work around the shoulder blades and a stretch under the arms.
stopIf: Pinching pain at the top of the shoulder.
